text.p: The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) said on Wednesday production at its "very profitable" new titanium dioxide project in southwest Australia was surging and should reach full output in the second half of 1997.
Commissioning of the A$230 million Beenup mining operation, one of a number of big investments expected to underpin BHP's future growth, began in December.

The project boasts annual design capacity of about 600,000 tonnes of ilmenite ore containing about 300,000 tonnes of titanium dioxide -- or about eight percent of world demand, said BHP's group general manager for titanium minerals, Ian Egan.
"The commissioning programme is going ahead of schedule," Egan told Reuters by telephone from Bunbury, the port where Beenup's ilmenite ore would be shipped to overseas markets.
A joint venture smelter in Norway, with BHP in partnership with Norwegian firm Tinfos AS, would take roughly half the ore, extracting titanium dioxide and iron as a by-product, Egan said.
The rest would be shipped to Japan, Europe and probably the United States, he added.
Titanium dioxide was used to make titanium pigments which were used extensively in the manufacture of paints, paper, plastics, inks and cosmetics.
The world market for pigment was worth around US$7 billion to A$8 billion each year, Egan said.
The Beenup mine was now operating at over half capacity, he said. "It's a huge mine...It's going very well," he added.
Egan was speaking before attending the official opening of the mine on Wednesday by Western Australia state Resources Development Minister Colin Barnett.

Egan said the Beenup mine's production costs were in the lowest quartile of world producers in terms of efficiency, and suggested margins were healthy given prevailing titanium dioxode prices of US$380 per tonne and iron prices at US$200 per tonne.
Ilmenite ore sells for US$80 per tonne, he said.
"It's a very profitable project," Egan said.
The Beenup deposit had an indicated resource of 83 million tonnes of ilmenite, giving it a mine life of over 100 years based on the current rate of production.
"Certainly it's the world's biggest undeveloped resource," Egan said. "The attraction is that we can increase production substantially over time," he added.
BHP expected Beenup to load its first shipments within about six weeks.
